It is the legal successor to the original [[General Electric]] Company founded in 1892, which split into three separate companies between November 2021 and April 2024, adopting the trade name GE Aerospace after divesting its healthcare ([[GE HealthCare]]) and energy ([[GE Vernova]]) divisions.{{cite news | last=Chesto | first=Jon | date=April 1, 2024 | url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/04/01/business/ge-split-three-companies-conglomerate/ | title=GE's long life as giant industrial conglomerate enters new era, as company splits up on Tuesday | work=The Boston Globe | archiveurl=https://archive.today/20240401214419/https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/04/01/business/ge-split-three-companies-conglomerate/ | archivedate=April 1, 2024 | url-status=live}}{{cite web | date=April 1, 2024 | last=Mazein | first=Elodie | url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/swan-song-general-electric-completes-015925420.html?guccounter=1 | title=Swan song for General Electric as it completes demerger | publisher=AFP | archiveurl=https://archive.today/20240402022206/https://www.yahoo.com/news/swan-song-general-electric-completes-015925420.html?guccounter=1 | archivedate=April 2, 2024 | via=Yahoo! News | quote=The official finalization of the separation comes Tuesday, with General Electric disappearing in favor of GE Vernova, dealing with energy activities, and GE Aerospace, the new name of the late GE. | url-status=live}} GE Aerospace both manufactures engines under its name and partners with other manufacturers to produce engines. [[CFM International]], the world's leading supplier of aircraft engines and GE's most successful partnership, is a 50/50 joint venture with the French company [[Safran Aircraft Engines]]. As of 2020, CFM International holds 39% of the world's commercial aircraft engine market share (while GE Aerospace itself holds a further 14%).{{Cite web |date=May 2021 |title=Market share of the leading commercial aircraft engine manufacturers worldwide in 2020 |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/1099835/global-aircraft-engine-manufacturer-market-share/ |access-date=22 November 2023 |website=[[Statista]] |language=en |archive-date=19 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230119141738/https://www.statista.com/statistics/1099835/global-aircraft-engine-manufacturer-market-share/ |url-status=live }} GE Aerospace's main competitors in the engine market are [[Pratt & Whitney]] and [[Rolls-Royce Holdings|Rolls-Royce]]. The division operated under the name of '''General Electric Aircraft Engines''' ('''GEAE''') until September 2005, and as '''GE Aviation''' until July 2022. In July 2022, GE Aviation changed its name to GE Aerospace in a move executives say reflects the engine maker's intention to broaden its focus beyond aircraft engines. In April 2024, GE Aerospace became the only business line of the former General Electric conglomerate, after it had completed the divestiture of [[GE HealthCare]] and [[GE Vernova]] (its energy businesses division).{{Cite web |last=Scott |first=Sean |title=GE Aviation, one of Greater Cincinnati's largest employers, to get new name |url=https://www.cincinnati.com/story/news/2022/07/18/ge-aviation-rebrands-ge-aerospace/10088342002/ |access-date=2024-01-11 |website=The Enquirer |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-01-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240111195159/https://www.cincinnati.com/story/news/2022/07/18/ge-aviation-rebrands-ge-aerospace/10088342002/ |url-status=live }} == History == === Early efforts === General Electric had a long history in steam turbine work, dating back to the 1900s. In 1903 they hired [[Sanford Alexander Moss]], who started the development of [[turbosupercharger]]s at GE. This led to a series of record-breaking flights over the next ten years. At first, the role of the high-altitude flight was limited, but in the years immediately prior to WWII they became standard equipment on practically all military aircraft.{{efn|By 1935, a '''Supercharger Division''' had been created at the River Works in [[Lynn, Massachusetts]].{{cite news |title=G.E. Receives Contract for Superchargers |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/946956181 |access-date=10 June 2026 |work=Daily Evening Item |date=29 December 1934 |page=2}}{{cite news |last1=Goodman |first1=Rebecca |title=Joseph Alford, Engineer at GE |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/102681263 |access-date=10 June 2026 |work=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=14 September 2004 |page=C4}}}} GE was a world leader in this technology; most other firms concentrated on the mechanically simpler supercharger driven by the engine itself, while GE had spent considerable effort developing the exhaust-driven turbo system that offered higher performance. This work made them the natural industrial partner to develop [[jet engine]]s when [[Frank Whittle]]'s [[Power Jets W.1|W.1]] engine was demonstrated to [[United States Army|U.S. Army]] General [[Hap Arnold]] in 1941.Leyes, p. 237 A production license was arranged in September, and several of the existing W.1 test engines shipped to the US for study, where they were converted to US manufacture as the [[General Electric I-A|I-A]]. GE quickly started production of improved versions; the I-16 ([[General Electric J31|J31]]) was produced in limited numbers starting in 1942, and the much more powerful I-40 (J33) followed in 1944, which went on to power the first US combat-capable jet fighters, the [[P-80 Shooting Star]]. Early jet engine work took place at Lynn, as well as GE's Syracuse, New York steam turbine plant, but soon concentrated at the former.Leyes, p. 238 On 31 July 1945 the Lynn plant became the '''Aircraft Gas Turbine Division'''.{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}} GE was repeatedly unable to deliver enough engines for Army and Navy demand, and production of the I-40 (now known as the [[Allison J33|J33]]) was also handed to [[Allison Engines]] in 1944. After the war ended, the Army canceled its orders for GE-built J33s and turned the entire production over to Allison,{{cite web|url=http://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/Allison-Gas-Turbine-Division-Company-History.html|title=History of Allison Gas Turbine Division|website=FundingUniverse|access-date=2009-05-20|archive-date=2012-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304024450/http://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/Allison-Gas-Turbine-Division-Company-History.html|url-status=live}} and the Syracuse plant closed. === Military and civilian expansion === [[File:General Electric J-47-27 USAF.jpg|thumb|The J47 had a production run of over 30,000.]] These changes in fortune led to debate within the company about carrying on in the aircraft engine market. However, the engineers at Lynn pressed ahead with the development of a new engine, the TG-180, which was designated [[Allison J35|J35]] by the US military.{{cite book|title=The Development of Jet and Turbine Engines|author=Bill Gunston|date=2006|edition=4th|publisher=Patrick Stephens|isbn=0-7509-4477-3|page=143}} Development funds were allotted in 1946 for a more powerful version of the same design, the TG-190. This engine finally emerged as the famed [[General Electric J47]], which saw a great demand for several military aircraft; a second manufacturing facility in [[Lockland, Ohio]], near [[Cincinnati]], was opened.{{efn|The plant is now known as "GE Evendale" after the [[Evendale, Ohio|Village of Evendale]], which was established in 1952.{{cite web |last1=Kennedy |first1=Rick |title=How GE’s "Magnificent Seven" Established the Evendale Complex |url=http://www.geaerospace.com/news/articles/100-year-anniversary/how-ges-magnificent-seven-established-evendale-complex |website=GE Aerospace |access-date=9 January 2026 |date=22 March 2019}}}}{{efn|The plant had originally been built for the Wright Aeronautical division of [[Curtiss-Wright]]. Ground was broken on 23 October 1940 and it was dedicated on 12 June 1941.{{cite news |title=Ground Broken for Wright Engine Plant |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/762211654 |access-date=4 May 2026 |work=Cincinnati Post |date=23 October 1940 |page=1}}{{cite news |last1=Koch |first1=Stanley |title=Wright Aero Plant Dedicated by Knudsen to Preservation of "Our Way of Life" |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/762239616 |access-date=4 May 2026 |work=Cincinnati Post |date=12 June 1941 |pages=1–2}}
Production at the plant began in 1948, but it was not officially opened until 28 February 1949, when the first two J47s were delivered to the Air Force.{{cite book |title=Eight Decades of Progress: A Heritage of Aircraft Turbine Technology |date=1990 |publisher=GE Aircraft Engines |location=Cincinnati, Ohio |page=65, 68 |lccn=90082948}}{{cite news |last1=Ruhl |first1=Frank J. |title=Air Force Accepts First Jet Power Engines Made at General Electric's Lockland Plant; U.S. Preparedness Stressed by Speakers |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/100542147 |access-date=9 January 2026 |date=1 March 1949 |page=22}} The plant itself was owned by [[Autolite|Electric Auto-Lite]] until it was purchased by GE in 1957. The latter did not take complete possession until the end of 1958.{{cite news |last1=Havlin |first1=Dick |title=GE is Buying Auto-Lite Plant in Deal of $15-$20 Million |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/102870949 |access-date=9 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=6 March 1957 |pages=1}}}} A strike in June 1952 exacerbated an existing delay in the production of J47s. Changes discovered as a result of flight testing had already resulted in new [[F-86]]s being parked due to a lack of engines.{{cite news |title=Major Walkout Likely at GE Plant |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/762790926 |access-date=23 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Post |date=18 June 1952 |page=1}}{{cite news |last1=Green |first1=Joe |title=Trickle of Engines Produced at GE Plant |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/100605295 |access-date=23 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=26 June 1952 |page=1}} After negotiations failed, an additional strike began in March 1953 and lasted until May.{{cite news |title=Strike Shuts GE Plant; Firm May Go to Court |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/762608435 |access-date=23 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Post |date=14 March 1953 |page=1}}{{cite news |title=General Electric Jet Plant Strike Settled |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/103290502 |access-date=23 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=18 May 1953 |page=1}} J47 production ran to 30,000 engines by the time the lines closed down in 1956. Further development of the J47 by led to the [[General Electric J73|J73]], and from there into the much more powerful [[General Electric J79|J79]]. The J79 was GE's second "hit", leading to a production run of 17,000 in several different countries. The GE and [[Lockheed Corporation|Lockheed]] team that developed the J79 and the [[F-104]] Mach 2 fighter aircraft received the 1958 [[Collier Trophy]] for outstanding technical achievement in aviation. Other successes followed, including the [[General Electric T58|T58]] and [[General Electric T64|T64]] [[turboshaft]] engines, the [[General Electric J85|J85]] turbojet, and [[General Electric F404|F404]] turbofan.{{Citation needed|date=January 2026}} The Aircraft Gas Turbine Division was renamed the '''Flight Propulsion Division''' in May 1959.{{cite news |title='Flight Propulsion Division;' New Name for GE in Evendale |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/100804560 |access-date=23 January 2026 |work=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=1 March 1959 |page=33-I}} Starting in 1961, General Electric started one of their most important research and development efforts, the GE1 technology demonstrator (originally designated the X101). The GE1 was a basic gas generator (compressor, combustor and turbine) onto which a variety of components such as fans, afterburners or other thrust vectoring devices could be added later. The design incorporated technologies such as a scaled compressor with variable stator vanes, an annular combustor, turbine-cooling advancements, and new materials for several government research programs. The US Government initially supported development of the GE1 to produce the [[General Electric J97|J97]] engine. The GE1 design and technology helped General Electric produce a range of engines, including the GE1/6 turbofan demonstrator for the [[General Electric TF39|TF39]] engine the [[General Electric GE4|GE4]] for the [[Boeing 2707]] supersonic airliner, and the GE9 engine for the USAF's Advanced Manned Strategic Aircraft, later [[General Electric F101|GE F101]] engines for the [[Rockwell B-1 Lancer|B-1]] bomber.{{cite book |title=Eight Decades of Progress: A Heritage of Aircraft Turbine Technology |date=1990 |publisher=GE Aircraft Engines |location=Cincinnati, Ohio |page=148 |lccn=90082948}}{{Cite web |last=Kennedy |first=Rick |date=2019-05-22 |title=GE1 "Building Block" Engine: Greatest GE Jet Engine Ever? |url=https://blog.geaviation.com/100-year-anniversary/ge1-building-block-engine-greatest-ge-jet-engine-ever/ |access-date=2022-05-06 |website=The GE Aviation Blog {{!}} Aerospace & Flight News |language=en-US |archive-date=2022-05-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220517183955/https://blog.geaviation.com/100-year-anniversary/ge1-building-block-engine-greatest-ge-jet-engine-ever/ |url-status=dead }} The [[General Electric F101]] was later developed into the [[General Electric F110]] and [[CFM International CFM56]] engines. The [[General Electric TF39|TF39]] was the first [[high-bypass turbofan engine]] to enter production.[http://www.geae.com/engines/commercial/cf6/index.html "The CF6 Engine Family"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110904041357/http://www.geae.com/engines/commercial/cf6/index.html |date=2011-09-04 }} Entered into the [[C-5 Galaxy]] contest in 1964 against similar designs from [[Curtiss-Wright]] and [[Pratt & Whitney]], GE's entry was selected as the winner during the final down-select in 1965. This led to a civilian model, the [[General Electric CF6|CF6]],{{Harvnb|Neumann|2004|pp=229–230}} which was offered for the [[Lockheed L-1011]] and [[McDonnell Douglas DC-10]] projects. Although Lockheed later changed their engine to the [[Rolls-Royce RB211]], the DC-10 continued with the CF6, and this success led to widespread sales on many large aircraft including the [[Boeing 747]]. Another military-to-civilian success followed when GE was selected to supply engines for the [[S-3 Viking]] and [[Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II]], developing a small high-bypass engine using technologies from the TF39. The resulting [[General Electric TF34|TF34]] was adapted to become the [[General Electric CF34|CF34]], whose wide variety of models powers many of the [[regional jet]]s flying today.{{Cite web |url=http://www.geae.com/engines/commercial/cf34/index.html |title=The CF34 Engine Family |access-date=2009-05-20 |archive-date=2011-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110824025310/http://www.geae.com/engines/commercial/cf34/index.html |url-status=dead }} As part of a reorganization of General Electric at the beginning of January 1968, the Flight Propulsion Division was renamed the '''Aircraft Engine Group'''.{{cite book |title=Seven Decades of Progress: A Heritage of Aircraft Turbine Technology |date=1979 |publisher=General Electric |isbn=0-8168-8355-6 |page=160 |url=http://www.archive.org/details/sevendecadesofpr0000gene |access-date=23 January 2026}} In the early 1970s, GE was also selected to develop a modern [[turboshaft]] engine for helicopter use, the [[General Electric T700|T700]]. It has been further developed as the [[General Electric T700|CT7]] turboprop engine for regional transports. === Commercial aviation powerplants === In 1974, GE entered into an agreement with [[Snecma]] of France, forming [[CFM International]] to jointly produce a new mid-sized turbofan, which emerged as the [[CFM56]]. A 50/50 joint partnership was formed{{Harvnb|Neumann|2004|p=234}} with a new plant in [[Evendale, OH]] to produce the design. At first, sales were very difficult to come by, and the project was due to be canceled. Only two weeks before this was to happen, in March 1979, several companies selected the CFM56 to re-engine their existing [[Douglas DC-8]] fleets.[http://www.cfm56.com/company/timeline "The CFM Timeline"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100323063956/http://www.cfm56.com/company/timeline |date=2010-03-23 }} GE announced it would be moving the headquarters of the Aircraft Engine Group from Lynn to Evendale that September.{{cite news |title=GE Realigns Aircraft Engine Group |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/947767771 |access-date=10 June 2026 |work=Daily Evening Item |date=18 September 1979 |pages=1, 11}} It was revealed in August 1986 that the group would be reorganized and an advanced technology division created.{{cite news |title=Change at Top of GE |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/948219613 |access-date=10 June 2026 |work=Daily Evening Item |date=4 August 1986 |pages=1, 8}} The success of the CFM led GE to join in several similar partnerships, including [[Garrett AiResearch]] for the [[CFE CFE738]], [[Pratt & Whitney]] on the [[Engine Alliance GP7000]], and, more recently, [[Honda]] for the [[GE Honda Aero Engines]] small turbofan project. GE also continued the development of its own lines, introducing new civilian models like the [[General Electric GE90|GE90]], and military designs like the [[General Electric F110]]. === GE Aerospace today === [[File:General Electric-747-N747GE-020918-03.jpg|thumb|General Electric used its 747-100 testbed in the 1990s for the GE90 which powers the Boeing 777-300ER, 777-200LR and 777F.]] GE and competitor Rolls-Royce were selected by [[Boeing Commercial Airplanes|Boeing]] to power its new [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner|787]]. GE Aviation's offering is the [[General Electric GEnx|GEnx]], a development of the GE90. The engine was also the exclusive power plant on the [[Boeing 747-8]]. The Lynn facility continues to assemble jet engines for the [[United States]] [[U.S. Department of Defense|Department of Defense]], subsidiary services, and commercial operators. Engines assembled at this plant include the [[General Electric F404|F404]], [[General Electric F414|F414]], [[General Electric T700|T700]], and [[General Electric CFE738|CFE738]]. The plant at Lynn also produces the -3 and -8 variants of the [[General Electric CF34|CF34]] regional jet engine, the CT7 commercial turboprop power plant, and commercial versions of the T700 turboshaft which are also called the CT7. The Evendale plant conducts final assembly for the [[CFM International]]'s [[CFM International CFM56|CFM56]], [[General Electric CF6|CF6]], as well as [[General Electric LM6000|LM6000]], and [[General Electric LM2500|LM2500]] power plants. [[File:VN-A861 LBG SIAE 2015 (18987933836).jpg|thumb|A [[General Electric GEnx|GEnx]] engine installed on the [[Boeing 787 Dreamliner|Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner]]]] The [[Durham, North Carolina]], facility conducts final assembly for the [[CFM International LEAP|CFM LEAP]], GEnx, CFM56, [[General Electric GE90|GE90]], GP7200, and [[General Electric CF34|CF34]] power plants. Crucial parts for these engines are crafted in secondary GE Aviation facilities, such as those in [[Bromont, Quebec]]; [[Hooksett, New Hampshire]]; [[Wilmington, North Carolina]]; [[Asheville, North Carolina]]; [[Madisonville, Kentucky]]; [[Rutland (city), Vermont|Rutland, Vermont]]; and [[Muskegon, Michigan]]; where the engine blades and vanes are manufactured. The division was briefly named '''GE Transportation Aircraft Engines''' in 1995 before becoming '''GE Aviation'''.{{cite news |last1=Newberry |first1=Jon |title=GE-Aviation Plans for Long Haul |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/766081583 |access-date=10 June 2026 |work=Cincinnati Post |date=29 October 2005 |page=8B}} [[Smiths Group]] and [[General Electric]] announced on January 15, 2007, that the former was divesting [[Smiths Aerospace]] to the latter for [[Pound sterling|£]]2.4 billion ([[United States dollar|US$]] 4.8 billion)."[https://www.wsj.com/article/BT-CO-20070115-703428.html Smiths To Sell Aerospace Ops To GE For $4.8B]{{dead link|date=July 2011}}." McGrath, S.; Stone, R. ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''. January 15, 2007. GE Aviation closed the transaction on May 4, 2007.{{cite press release|url=http://www.smiths-aerospace.com/News/Archive/2007/GE-Aviatio/index.asp|title=GE Aviation Completes Acquisition of Smiths Aerospace|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071031232515/http://www.smiths-aerospace.com/News/Archive/2007/GE-Aviatio/index.asp |archive-date=2007-10-31|website=Smiths Aerospace|date=May 4, 2007}} Smiths Aerospace, which was an important supplier, became an operating subsidiary of GE Aviation known as [[GE Aviation Systems]]. This acquisition will reportedly give the combined unit the clout to resist pricing pressures from its two largest customers, [[Boeing Commercial Airplanes|Boeing]] and [[Airbus]]. Analysts further assert that it enables General Electric to acquire assets similar to those it desired in its failed bid for [[Honeywell]] in 2000. Along with the purchase of Smiths Aerospace, the purchase included opening the first [[University Development Center]] at [[Michigan Technological University]] in [[Houghton, Michigan]], in the effort to work with engineering students to provide training in engineering and software development. The program has performed well and GE Aviation has announced further UDC openings at [[Kansas State University]]. In July 2008, governments in the [[Persian Gulf]] reached agreements with GE to expand engine maintenance operations there. The [[Wall Street Journal]] reported that [[Mubadala Development Company]], which owns Abu Dhabi Aircraft Technologies, an overhaul, and maintenance company, signed an agreement worth an estimated $8 billion with GE; Abu Dhabi Aircraft Technologies will maintain and overhaul GE engines used in commercial aircraft purchased by airlines based in the Persian Gulf.Mideast Widens Aircraft Ventures, Wall Street Journal, July 30, 2008, p. B2. By July 2010, CFM International had delivered their 21,000th engine of the CFM56 family, with an ongoing production rate of 1250 per year, against a four-year production backlog.{{cite press release|url=http://www.geaviation.com/press/cfm56/cfm56-x/cfm56-x_20101116d.html|title=CFM Delivers 21,000th CFM56 Engine While Retaining Solid Delivery Backlog|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309040307/http://www.geaviation.com/press/cfm56/cfm56-x/cfm56-x_20101116d.html |archive-date=2016-03-09|access-date=November 16, 2010}} On December 23, 2012, GE announced that it has agreed to purchase the aeronautical division of [[Avio]], an Italy-based manufacturer of aviation propulsion components and systems for civil and military aircraft, for $4.3 billion U.S. (EUR3.3 billion)."{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130117125135/http://www.avionics-intelligence.com/news/2012/12/24/ge-to-acquire-aviation-business-of-avio-s-p-a.html|title=GE Announces purchase of Avio S.p.A}}" GE Aviation follows through to develop a [[supersonic]] engine concept for [[Aerion]] with a configuration accommodating reasonably well requirements for supersonic speed, subsonic speed and noise levels.{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/nbaa-ge-nears-milestones-on-15b-bet-on-business-a-441992/ |title= GE nears milestones on $1.5B bet on business aircraft |date= 10 Oct 2017 |author= Stephen Trimble |work= Flightglobal |archive-date= 10 October 2017 |access-date= 10 October 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171010075621/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/nbaa-ge-nears-milestones-on-15b-bet-on-business-a-441992/ |url-status= live }} On July 18, 2022, GE announced that GE Aviation had been renamed '''GE Aerospace''',{{cite web|url=https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2022-07-19/new-ge-aerospace-unit-laser-focused-airline-recovery|title=New GE Aerospace Unit Laser-focused on Airline Recovery|last=Alcock|first=Charles|date=July 19, 2022|work=AIN Online|publisher=AIN Media Group, Inc|access-date=May 22, 2023|archive-date=May 22, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230522201619/https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2022-07-19/new-ge-aerospace-unit-laser-focused-airline-recovery|url-status=live}} and would become the successor to the GE company once the spinoffs of its subsidiaries are completed. GE Aerospace will own the GE trademark and logo, and will license the brand to the other companies, [[GE HealthCare]] and [[GE Vernova]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.geaerospace.com/news/press-releases/other-news-information/ge-unveils-brand-names-three-planned-future-public-companies|title=GE Unveils Brand Names for Three Planned Future Public Companies | GE Aerospace News|website=www.geaerospace.com|access-date=2024-08-09|archive-date=2024-08-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240809193248/https://www.geaerospace.com/news/press-releases/other-news-information/ge-unveils-brand-names-three-planned-future-public-companies|url-status=live}} ==== Additive manufacturing ==== Recently, they have started incorporating 3D printing technologies in their engines and have incorporated the manufacturing process in the newly designed [[General Electric GE9X|GE9X]], the largest jet engine in the world.Scott, Clare. [https://3dprint.com/131192/ge-aviation-big-jet-engine/ "GE Aviation Tests the Largest Jet Engine in the World, Featuring 3D Printed Fuel Nozzles"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160426185423/https://3dprint.com/131192/ge-aviation-big-jet-engine/ |date=2016-04-26 }}, ''3D Print'', 25 April 2016. Accessed 16 May 2016. GE acquired [[Arcam]] EBM for [[electron beam melting]], Concept Laser for [[laser melting]], and material provider AP&C. [[Metal casting]] improves through competition with metal [[additive manufacturing]], for which GE Additive believes it will soon compete with metal [[forging]] which will then be enhanced in response. Additive manufacturing is focused on new builds but can be used for part replacement: when complexity rise, costs can stays level – for example, replacing a turbine consisting of 300 components with one piece. The electron beam melting has good speed for economy, [[Engineering tolerance|precision]] to reduce processing work, and size capability for larger parts; the hot process reduces [[Mechanical stress|stresses]] in the part and penetrates deeper than laser for thicker parts with coarser, cheaper [[metal powder]]s. Additive techniques can be used across the engine and even in the over {{cvt|1,500|°F|°C}} hot section. They are used in the [[General Electric CT7|CT7]] [[combustor]] liner, for [[GE9X]] low pressure [[turbine blade]]s – the first rotating parts – and for 16 parts in the [[General Electric Advanced Turboprop|ATP]], including an 80 parts [[heat exchanger]] consolidated into one.{{cite news |url= http://www.mro-network.com/emerging-technology/additive-manufacturing-could-disrupt-lot-aerospace-markets |title= Additive Manufacturing Could Disrupt |author= Henry Canaday |date= Dec 11, 2017 |work= Aviation Week Network |archive-date= December 11, 2017 |access-date= December 11, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20171211150913/http://www.mro-network.com/emerging-technology/additive-manufacturing-could-disrupt-lot-aerospace-markets |url-status= live }} == Products == === Turbojets === [[File:General Electric J79.jpg|thumb|[[General Electric J79]]]] {| class="wikitable sortable" |- ! General Electric Company, doing business as GE Aerospace, is an American aircraft engine supplier that is headquartered in Evendale, Ohio, outside Cincinnati. It is the legal successor to the original General Electric Company founded in 1892, which split into three separate companies between November 2021 and April 2024, adopting the trade name GE Aerospace after divesting its healthcare (GE HealthCare) and energy (GE Vernova) divisions.
GE Aerospace both manufactures engines under its name and partners with other manufacturers to produce engines. CFM International, the world's leading supplier of aircraft engines and GE's most successful partnership, is a 50/50 joint venture with the French company Safran Aircraft Engines. As of 2020, CFM International holds 39% of the world's commercial aircraft engine market share (while GE Aerospace itself holds a further 14%). GE Aerospace's main competitors in the engine market are Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce.
The division operated under the name of General Electric Aircraft Engines (GEAE) until September 2005, and as GE Aviation until July 2022. In July 2022, GE Aviation changed its name to GE Aerospace in a move executives say reflects the engine maker's intention to broaden its focus beyond aircraft engines. In April 2024, GE Aerospace became the only business line of the former General Electric conglomerate, after it had completed the divestiture of GE HealthCare and GE Vernova (its energy businesses division).
